title: Taming AI Agents with Capsem: Hardware Sandboxing That Doesn't Kill Productivity

speakers.name: Elie Bursztein
speakers.affiliation: Distinguished Research Scientist, Google DeepMind (slides carry the Google Security and Privacy Research mark)

thesis: Agent security fails when it is pitted against velocity, so the sandbox must be the fastest and easiest way to run agents, with the security boundary pushed down into a Rust hypervisor, per-VM low-privilege subprocesses and a single policy-enforcing egress point, the way Chrome won by being fast first and secure by design.
summary: Bursztein opens with the familiar boardroom standoff between security and speed and argues the community must stop framing it as a trade-off. His answer is Capsem, an open-source Rust hypervisor, about nine months old, that boots hardened Linux VMs running OCI containers for agents such as Claude Code, Codex CLI, Antigravity and Claude Desktop, with a one-click install, CLI, UI, SDKs and MCP server, and, he says, under two second boot. He explains the secure-by-default design: each agent in its own zero-trust VM, no direct network, and a pile of small sandboxed subprocesses (Landlock and seccomp) in the style of Chrome. Networking is split into three paths: LAN and internet traffic through a per-VM security engine that man-in-the-middles HTTPS with an injected root certificate; inter-VM traffic through a pure Rust virtual layer-2 router; and exposed developer ports through an authenticated low-privilege process. The security engine runs plugins (credential broker, PII scanner, input sanitizer, malware scanner in progress) and rules written in TOML with CEL (Common Expression Language) expressions over IP, TCP, DNS, HTTP, model, MCP, file and process events, plus Sigma detections and OpenTelemetry output. A planned demo video failed. He then reports lessons from building Capsem entirely with AI agents: tests are 52 percent of the code, guardrail rules catch repeated agent mistakes, yet CI success rate collapsed and releases slowed from 20 minutes to three to four hours.
argument: Security and velocity must stop being opposed, because teams will not accept extra steps and the agent wave will not slow down.
The right place for control is the environment: push the security boundary down into a sandbox that is more convenient and faster than the unsandboxed alternative, as Chrome did for browsing.

A secure agent sandbox needs per-agent zero-trust VMs, an air gap behind a single policy-enforcing egress point with full semantic visibility (HTTP, model, MCP), and a modular set of low-privilege subprocesses instead of a monolith.
Policy must be expressive, enforceable at the right stack level, and authorable by agents, and observability should plug into enterprise standards (Sigma, OpenTelemetry).
Building such a system with AI agents is feasible but costly in testing and release engineering, and the AI's repeated rule violations make release speed collapse.

claims.claim: Capsem boots fully configured agent VMs in about two seconds and supports multiple concurrent sessions.
claims.evidence: Stated by the speaker and on the Ship fast slide (under 2 secs); a dashboard screenshot shows running sessions but no timing was demonstrated because the demo video did not play.

claims.claim: Capsem is about 630,000 lines of Rust-centered code with 14,926 tests.
claims.evidence: Key numbers on the architecture slide (speaker said about 600,000 lines and over 15,000 tests).

claims.claim: The security engine sustains about 5,000 requests per second from inside the VM with sub-1ms event processing including reconstruction.
claims.evidence: Benchmark figure stated and shown on the Security engine slide; no methodology, hardware or payload size given.

claims.claim: Every VM gets its own security engine process as the single egress point, so a compromised engine cannot relay traffic across VMs.
claims.evidence: Architecture description and diagram of per-VM processes with security engine A and B.

claims.claim: HTTPS can be inspected transparently because Capsem controls the patched VM and injects a root certificate, forging certificates on demand and caching them.
claims.evidence: Design explanation; no verification of bypass resistance shown.

claims.claim: Inter-VM networking uses a pure Rust virtual layer-2 switch that avoids the host kernel, reaching about 2 GB per second.
claims.evidence: Speaker's description (ARP routing and broadcast in a low-privilege process); throughput figure spoken only and unverified.

claims.claim: Exposing a VM port to the host browser creates a same-origin risk between VMs and a local-file access risk; a not fully exploitable local-file bug was found in that component.
claims.evidence: Speaker's account of bugs found; this subsystem was where they found the most bugs.

claims.claim: A credential broker replaces real credentials with placeholder values so the agent in the VM never sees them.
claims.evidence: Plugin described and listed on the Key security plugins slide.

claims.claim: Rules can be written as TOML with CEL expressions over ip, tcp, udp, dns, http, model, mcp, files and process events, with actions allow, ask, deny and rewrite.
claims.evidence: Rule examples shown: a block rule on a model response containing London, and an allow rule for local Ollama on 127.0.0.1:11434.

claims.claim: Sigma detection rules compile to Capsem rules, enabling real-time detection and blocking on file, process and network events visible to the hypervisor.
claims.evidence: Example rule for logging when a SKILL.md file is read; stated as compiled and marked to log.

claims.claim: Hypervisor code is about 2 percent of the codebase, tests are 52 percent and guardrail rules about 6 to 7 percent, with the rest including build and release.
claims.evidence: Donut chart from docs.capsem.org/architecture/statistics; the chart labels both Tests and Build and Release as 52.3 percent, while the speaker said the build system was about 5 percent.

claims.claim: The AI-driven development process eroded release reliability: the CI successful-run rate fell from roughly 24 to 26 percent in spring 2026 to about 4 percent in August, and releases slowed from about 20 minutes to three to four hours in the best case.
claims.evidence: Line chart of successful rate by month labeled release system collapse; the speaker said July success was literally zero while the chart minimum is about 4 percent in August.

claims.claim: The coding agent repeatedly makes violating changes, such as switching a required binary protocol to JSON (collapsing performance and adding vulnerability), duplicating file I/O abstractions, forgetting to push binaries, and a fork path where some events skipped the security system.
claims.evidence: Anecdotes from development; guardrail rules were written after each mistake.

claims.claim: Enterprise customers' hardest problem is shadow IT: they are unsure what agents and tokens are running, and creating a new agent binary takes about 20 minutes of vibe coding, so binaries explode.
claims.evidence: Feedback from the speaker's conversations with large Google Cloud clients; no data.

frameworks.name: Fast, usable, secure triangle
frameworks.description: Design goal that Capsem must satisfy all three; insight is a specialized agent environment, think Chrome for agents.

frameworks.name: Secure by default pillars
frameworks.description: Four cards: zero-trust environment (each agent in an isolated hardened VM), air-gapped (all traffic through the security engine), policy engine (HTTP, DNS, model, MCP, file, process detection and rule enforcement), security plugins (API to intercept, block, ask and rewrite events).

frameworks.name: Split networking subsystem
frameworks.description: Three isolated paths: LAN and internet through the per-VM security engine process; inter-VM through a sandboxed pure Rust virtual router; exposed ports through an authenticated sandboxed low-privilege process.

frameworks.name: Fine-grained sandboxed subprocesses
frameworks.description: Components colored by host permission: minimum (granted connections only), limited (assigned files, credentials or upstream connections), elevated (VM control), maximum (launching-user permissions), with a VM hardware boundary around the OCI container and guest helpers, and a per-VM ownership boundary.

frameworks.name: Policy design problems
frameworks.description: Three decisions every policy system faces: expressivity (including quantifying over history), the stack level to enforce at (IP and TCP, DNS, HTTP via man-in-the-middle, model bodies, MCP semantics), and the authoring system (a typed programming-language DSL that agents can autocomplete and compile-check).

slide_only: Disclaimer slide: Capsem is 100% AI code generated.

Why users love Capsem: easy to start (single click install, catalogue of agents), ready to go (popular agents, standard tools and environments), versatile (CLI for cloud set-up, UI for laptops, SDKs and MCP for remote and complex use cases).

Product definition slide: high-performance Rust hypervisor that runs concurrent OCI containers in specialized hardened Linux VMs with network air gap, advanced security controls and enterprise-grade observability.
Stack diagram: Native App (rust + js), MCP (typescript), CLI (rust) and System Tray (rust) on top of SDKs, then the hypervisor, then VM plus container instances.

Process diagram components include capsem-gateway, capsem-service, capsem-process, capsem-router Expose, Security engine, capsem-mcp-aggregator, capsem-mcp-builtin, Log writer capsem-ledger, guest helpers and an external MCP servers box.

Security engine pipeline diagram: VM traffic or standalone API model requests, network analysis engine producing a SecurityEvent, preprocess plugins, rule evaluation with CEL conditions, postprocess plugins, effective decision (refuse or await approval versus prepare request and restore credentials), logging plugins sanitizing events to a session database or archive; TOML rule files and Sigma YAML detection files feed rule compilation.
Security engine slide: single low privileged egress point; full ip, tcp, http, model and mcp semantic inspection and enforcement; 100 percent of events routed to the logging process.
Plugin cards: credential broker, PII scanner, sanitizer that normalizes model input to remove non-ASCII and other weirdness, malware scanner marked WIP scanning inbound and outbound URLs and files.

Enforcement rule slide shows two TOML profiles with priority fields (block_london at priority 10, allow_local_ollama at priority 20) and the CEL field list ip, tcp, udp, dns, http, model, mcp, files, process.

Sigma example titled skill_loaded at informational level: logsource product capsem service security_event, selection file.read.name SKILL.md and file.read.ext md, capsem action allow with reason record when an agent skill file is loaded.

Why enterprise loves Capsem: fully customizable (profiles, VM images, rules, detections self-authored and deployed), fully observable (OpenTelemetry aware reporting), real time detection (Sigma compliant), instant remediation response (security engine and API for local or remote response).

offense: Prompt injection and agents acting beyond their remit are the motivating threats; the talk names sandbox escapes by models as a recent proof that weak environments fail.
Exposed VM ports create a same-origin problem between VMs and a path to local host files if not restricted.
A compromised egress process could relay traffic across VMs if shared, which motivates one security engine per VM.
Non-ASCII or unusual characters in prompts are treated as attack surface for prompt injection.
defense: Run each agent in its own hardened VM with no direct network, using Rust components with Landlock and seccomp (and seccomp on macOS) around each subprocess.
Route all egress through one low-privilege security engine per VM with full ip, tcp, http, model and mcp inspection and complete logging.
Use a credential broker so real credentials never enter the VM, plus PII scanning and a sanitizer that strips non-ASCII and odd characters from model input.
Write rules as typed TOML plus CEL conditions with allow, ask, deny, rewrite actions, enforce corporate rules first via a manifest, and emit OpenTelemetry events.
Ingest Sigma detections for file, process, network and model events and use the API for instant local or remote remediation.
Keep inter-VM links explicit decisions, and restrict and authenticate exposed ports.
Write guardrail rules for the coding agent after each recurring mistake and run end-to-end install and boot tests inside a fresh VM before release.
takeaways: As a design bet with no adoption data shown, make the sandboxed path the fastest way to start an agent; adoption, not mandate, is what will make a boundary stick.
As a design to test, put control at the environment boundary with a single egress choke point that understands model and MCP semantics, not just IP and DNS.
As a design to test, hide long-lived credentials from agents with a broker and treat unusual characters in prompts as a cheap hardening control.
On one project's evidence, if agents write your code, budget for a large test and guardrail investment and expect release engineering to slow; measure CI success rate as a health signal.
On anecdote from customer conversations, solve shadow-IT visibility alongside sandboxing, because enterprises cannot enforce a sandbox on agent binaries they cannot find.
limits: Capsem is 100 percent AI-generated; the team reviews and tests but acknowledges AI introduces mistakes and sometimes assumption-violating changes.
Release process and reliability degraded significantly as the project grew.
OpenTelemetry support is by default but has not been tested much and may have bugs; the malware scanner is work in progress; the policy authoring language is not yet deployed.
Enforcing use of a single environment (on Mac, Windows) across an enterprise is unsolved, and vendors will have to help.
The speaker does not claim Capsem has the best policy solution, only a list of the hard problems.
critique: No security evaluation is shown: no escape testing, red-team results, threat model coverage or comparison to other sandboxes (gVisor, Firecracker, Kata were raised only in Q&A), so the secure-by-default claims rest on architecture description in the recording.

Man-in-the-middle HTTPS inspection with a root certificate injected into every guest concentrates trust in the security engine and its certificate cache; no verification of bypass resistance was shown, and no data on certificate pinning, non-HTTP exfiltration channels or covert channels.
Speed and throughput numbers (two second boot, 5,000 RPS, 2 GB per second) lack methodology, and the boot claim was not demonstrated because the demo video failed.

The AI-development retrospective covers a single project, and the chart labels differ from each other and from the speaker's description (a July zero versus an August minimum near 4 percent, Tests and Build both 52.3 percent).
The slides state 'users love' and 'enterprise loves' Capsem; no adoption data was shown.
qa: Q: How does Capsem relate to other sandbox technologies like gVisor and Kata? A: Much legacy technology will be rewritten; sandboxes written before Rust differ from Rust ones (Firecracker, Nitro and others), C++ is a liability for security code, and there will be an explosion of sandboxes with a race on performance and usability; sandboxes need low-privilege subprocesses rather than monoliths and real isolation between VMs.

Q: What enterprise feedback have you had, and is it painful to move a working directory into a sandbox? A: Through talks with large Google Cloud customers the main concern is not knowing what agents and token spend exist in the organization (shadow IT); enforcing a single environment on Mac and Windows is hard, agent binaries multiply because a new one takes about 20 minutes of vibe coding, and compliance and deployment are harder than the technology.

Q: How do you manage policies so users can just get work done? A: Policy systems hit three problems: expressivity (needing to quantify over the history of tools and model calls, with CEL as a sweet spot between regex and formal logic, relevant to the no private data plus internet access plus destruction combination), enforcement level (IP and TCP are easy, then DNS, then HTTP needing man-in-the-middle, then model bodies and MCP with differing provider formats), and authoring (use a programming-language-based thin DSL such as JavaScript objects so agents can autocomplete and compilers can check). Easiness, speed and expressivity form the trade-off triangle.

signal.reason: The talk describes an open-source Rust sandbox architecture, policy-design lessons and a retrospective on building the project with AI agents, with no security evaluation shown and a demo video that did not play.

caveats: The captions say CapSentry, Cap Sam, Kapsel and Captum; the slides say Capsem, and this record uses the slides.
The speaker said 600,000 lines and over 15,000 tests; the slides say 630,247 and 14,926, and this record uses the slides.
The code-share donut labels Build and Release as 52.3 percent, same as Tests; the speaker said about 5 percent, so the Build and Release figure is unreliable.
The speaker said CI success hit literally zero in July; the chart's lowest point is about 4 percent in August. Chart values were read from the image.
The demo video failed to play, so no live demonstration is recorded.
The opening news headlines were shown without comment; their details (Hugging Face hack, OpenAI agents) are recorded only as slide content and not verified.
The captions give the inter-VM throughput as two gigabytes per second; no slide shows it, so the claim about it rests on speech alone.
